title: Numbers & shopping
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Korean has TWO complete sets of numbers and the job decides which one you use. The Sino-Korean set (il, i, sam, sa, o …) counts money, minutes and dates. The native Korean set (hana, dul, set, net …) counts things and hours. Nothing in English prepares you for this, and there is no way to get by with one of them.

A counter is not optional. Korean cannot say 'two coffees' — it says keopi du jan, 'coffee two cups'. The order is noun, then number, then counter, and every countable thing needs one: -gae for objects, -myeong for people, -jan for cupfuls.

The first four native numbers SHRINK in front of a counter: hana becomes han, dul becomes du, set becomes se, net becomes ne. It is not a casual variant — han gae is the only way to say 'one thing', and hana gae is simply wrong.
Prices are Sino-Korean and won never takes a plural: samcheon won, ocheon won. The numbers are built by stacking pieces — sam plus cheon is three-thousand — and they are written and said as one word.

myeot ('how many') goes exactly where a number goes, in front of the counter: sagwa-ga myeot gae isseoyo? Like eodi it does not move to the front of the sentence, and the question is still made by the voice.
The counted phrase sits where the plain noun sat, and the noun keeps its marker: keopi-reul du jan juseyo. The number and counter follow the marked noun rather than replacing anything.

sentences.glossEn: Please give me two cups of coffee.

words.note: 'Coffee', from M1 — counted here in cups.
'Two', native Korean, and it shortens the same way: dul alone, du in front of a counter. The first four numbers all do this, and nothing else in the set does.
The counter for a cupful — coffee, tea, water. keopi du jan is 'two coffees'. It is the word for a cup as well, which is why it counts them.
'Please give me', from M3. In an order the counted phrase comes before it, exactly where the plain object stood: keopi-reul du jan juseyo.

sentences.trap: English puts the number in front of the thing and pluralises it. Korean puts the noun first with its marker, then the number, then a word saying what KIND of thing is being counted — three pieces where English has two.
sentences.sound: KUH-pee-rul du jan JOO-se-yo. du is one short beat and jan another; do not run them together, because the pair is doing two different jobs.

variations.changed: one instead of two, and hana has shrunk to han
a different drink in the same cups
three, and set has shrunk to se

mistake.why: The counter has been left out and the full form of the number used. Both halves are wrong together: a counted thing needs its counter, and in front of one the number shrinks.

sentences.mnemonic: Noun, number, counter — in that order, every time.

words.note: 'This one', from M1 — what you are pointing at in a shop.
'How much is it?'. Look at the end of it: -yeyo, M1's copula on a noun meaning 'how much'. Korean asks 'it is how much?' and the whole question is one word plus a rise.

sentences.trap: This is M1's copula doing shopping. eolmayeyo is a noun meaning 'how much' with -yeyo on the end, so the question is literally 'this is how much?' — there is no verb here meaning 'to cost'.
sentences.sound: EE-guh-nun UL-ma-yeh-yo, rising at the end. Four beats in eolmayeyo, all light; the eo at the front is the same vowel as in jeo.

variations.changed: a named thing rather than one you are pointing at
the same question about a drink
the answer, with a price where eolma stood

mistake.why: The existence verb has been used to ask a price. eolma takes the copula, because you are asking what the thing IS, not whether it is there.

sentences.usage: Asking a price for anything at all.
sentences.mnemonic: A price is something a thing IS.

words.note: 'Three thousand', built from the Sino-Korean numbers: sam ('three') plus cheon ('thousand'). Money is always counted with this set, and the pieces are written together as one word, which is how they are said.
The Korean currency. It never takes a plural — samcheon won, not 'thousands of wons' — and prices are always said with the Sino-Korean numbers, never the native ones.

sentences.trap: won never becomes plural. English says 'three thousand wons' by reflex and Korean has no plural to reach for — the number does all the counting there is.
sentences.sound: SAM-chun WUH-nee-eh-yo. The n of won links into the -ieyo, so it is heard as wuh-ni-e-yo. samcheon is two beats and is said as one word, because it is one.

variations.cue: The apples are three thousand won.
variations.changed: the thing named as well as the price
the same words with a rise — checking the price

mistake.why: The native number has been used for money. Prices are Sino-Korean: samcheon, not set-cheon, and the two sets never mix inside one number.

sentences.mnemonic: Money counts in the other set, and never in the plural.

words.note: 'Apple'. It is the module's countable thing, so it appears with gae in most of these sentences.
'Three', native Korean, shortening to se in front of a counter. Learn the pair together — set for counting, se for counting things.
The all-purpose counter for objects. Korean cannot say 'three apples': it says 'apples three gae', and gae is what you use for anything that has no counter of its own.
'Please give me', from M3. In an order the counted phrase comes before it, exactly where the plain object stood: keopi-reul du jan juseyo.

sentences.trap: gae is the counter you use when a thing has no counter of its own, and most things do not. It is the safe one — but it is never right for people.
sentences.sound: SA-gwa-rul se gae JOO-se-yo. se and gae are two short, separate beats. sagwa's gwa is one syllable, a g followed by the wa glide.

variations.changed: one, with hana shrunk to han
two, with dul shrunk to du
a different object taking the same all-purpose counter

mistake.why: The marker has been moved onto the number. It belongs to the noun — sagwa-reul — and the number and counter follow the marked noun without markers of their own.

sentences.usage: Buying a countable number of anything.
sentences.mnemonic: gae counts things, and most things are things.

sentences.glossEn: There are two friends. · I have two friends.

words.note: 'Friend', from M1 — counted here with the counter for people.
'Two', native Korean, and it shortens the same way: dul alone, du in front of a counter. The first four numbers all do this, and nothing else in the set does.
The counter for people. chingu du myeong is 'two friends'. Using gae for a person is not merely wrong, it is rude — people have their own counter and it is this one.
'There is', from M3, counting here rather than merely existing.

sentences.trap: People have their own counter. Using gae for a person is not a small error — it counts them as objects — so myeong is worth learning as a separate fact rather than as one item in a list.
sentences.sound: CHIN-goo-ga du MYUNG i-SSUH-yo. myeong is one beat with the eo vowel and a held ng at the end.

variations.changed: one person

variations.cue: How many friends do you have?
variations.changed: the question, with myeot where the number stood

mistake.why: People have been counted with the counter for objects. It is grammatical and it is rude — myeong exists precisely so that people are not counted as things.

sentences.usage: Saying how many people there are.

words.note: 'Apple'. It is the module's countable thing, so it appears with gae in most of these sentences.
'How many'. It goes where a number would go, in front of the counter: myeot gae, 'how many things'. Like eodi, it does not move to the front of the sentence — the voice does the asking.
The all-purpose counter for objects. Korean cannot say 'three apples': it says 'apples three gae', and gae is what you use for anything that has no counter of its own.
'There is', from M3, counting here rather than merely existing.

sentences.trap: myeot does not move to the front. English has to lead with 'how many'; Korean leaves it exactly where the number would be, and the rise at the end does the asking.
sentences.sound: SA-gwa-ga myut GAE i-SSUH-yo, rising at the end. myeot ends in an unreleased t that runs straight into the g of gae, so the pair comes out as myut-kae.

mistake.why: myeot has been fronted the way English fronts 'how many', and the counter dropped. It goes in the number's seat, in front of the counter, and the counter has to be there.

sentences.usage: Asking how many of something there are.
sentences.mnemonic: Ask where the answer will be.

sentences.cue: The tea is five thousand won.
sentences.glossEn: As for the tea, it is five thousand won.

words.note: 'Tea', from M1, priced here rather than drunk.
'Five thousand' — o ('five') plus cheon ('thousand'), from the same Sino-Korean set as samcheon. Once you have the pieces, every price between them is built the same way.
The Korean currency. It never takes a plural — samcheon won, not 'thousands of wons' — and prices are always said with the Sino-Korean numbers, never the native ones.

sentences.trap: The topic marker here does what it always does — sets the tea apart from the other things on the menu. In a shop that is exactly what you want: this one, as opposed to the others.
sentences.sound: CHA-nun O-chun WUH-nee-eh-yo. ocheon is two beats, o and cheon, and the whole price runs into the copula as one flow.

variations.cue: The coffee is three thousand won.

the question this sentence answers

variations.cue: The apples are five thousand won.

mistake.why: The existence verb again where the copula belongs. A price is what a thing IS: won-ieyo, not won isseoyo, which would say the tea has five thousand won on it.

sentences.usage: Answering a price question about one item.
sentences.mnemonic: -neun picks this one out; the copula says what it is.

sentences.glossEn: Please give me one cup of coffee.

words.note: 'Coffee', from M1 — counted here in cups.
'One', in the native Korean numbers — the set used for counting things. It has two shapes: hana when you count on its own, han when a counter follows. The short shape is not optional.
The counter for a cupful — coffee, tea, water. keopi du jan is 'two coffees'. It is the word for a cup as well, which is why it counts them.
'Please give me', from M3. In an order the counted phrase comes before it, exactly where the plain object stood: keopi-reul du jan juseyo.

sentences.trap: hana becomes han and there is no choice about it. This is the shrinking rule at its sharpest, because hana is the number a learner knows best and the one they will reach for first.
sentences.sound: KUH-pee-rul han jan JOO-se-yo. han and jan rhyme and are said as two even beats; the n of han is fully pronounced before the j.
